title: Benchmark an agent with state-checked tasks
summary: Build a small tau-bench-style benchmark for a customer-support agent. Each trial gets a fresh SQLite shop, tools that deliberately do not enforce the policy, and a simulated user who reveals facts only when asked. Success means the database ends in exactly the right state and the trajectory obeyed the rules. You will measure pass^k, see how reliability collapses as k grows, label every failure, and then benchmark a real model through any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
outcome: A Python package `bench` with nine tasks, end-state and trajectory checks, a reference agent, a seeded sloppy agent that makes realistic mistakes, an LLM agent adapter, a runner, a pass^k report with failure categories, and sixteen passing tests.
prereqs: The agent evals and harness lessons of this track

tools.name: SQLite
tools.why: a fresh in-memory shop database per trial

tools.name: pytest
tools.why: tests that pin down tasks, checks and fault labels

steps.text: Understand the design before writing code: the environment holds state, tasks describe a goal and the exact end state that counts as success, checks compare the two and inspect the trajectory, and agents are interchangeable. Anything you can wrap in an agent's run(env, user) method can be benchmarked.

phases.title: The environment and the simulated user
phases.goal: A fresh, deterministic shop per trial with tools and a call log, and a user who answers only what is asked.

steps.text: Write the environment. The date is fixed so results are reproducible, every tool call is logged, and the policy lives in text the agent reads.

Notice that refund_order and update_address do not check the policy. That is deliberate and realistic: back-office APIs rarely encode every business rule, so following the policy is part of what the benchmark measures.
Try the environment by hand: a refund without verification changes the database exactly as expected, but the checks still fail it on the trajectory rule.

code.code:
uv run python -c "
from bench.tasks import TASKS
from bench.checks import check, diff
task = TASKS[0]
env = task.make_env()
print(env.find_customer('ana@example.com'))
print(env.refund_order('O-1001'))
print(diff(env))
print(check(task, env, 'done'))
"

steps.text: Write the simulated user. It opens with a vague request and reveals one fact (email, zip, order number, address) only when a question asks for it, so an agent that guesses instead of asking fails.

code.code:
# src/bench/user.py
"""A rule-based simulated user: reveals one fact only when asked for it."""

import re


class SimUser:
    def __init__(self, opening: str, facts: dict[str, str]):
        self.opening, self.facts, self.turns = opening, facts, 0

    def reply(self, question: str) -> str:
        self.turns += 1
        q = question.lower()
        for key, pattern in [
            ("email", r"e-?mail"),
            ("zip", r"zip|post ?code"),
            ("order_id", r"order"),
            ("address", r"address"),
        ]:
            if re.search(pattern, q) and key in self.facts:
                return self.facts[key]
        return "Sorry, I'm not sure what you need. " + self.opening

phases.title: Tasks and checks
phases.goal: Nine tasks with exact expected end states, and checks that also catch unverified writes and actions the task did not need.

steps.text: Write the tasks. Most of them expect no change at all: a late refund, a shipped order, a wrong zip code, an already-refunded order, another customer's order. Refusing correctly is as important as acting correctly.

code.code:
# src/bench/tasks.py
"""Tasks: who the user is, what they want, and the exact end state that counts as success."""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

from .env import ShopEnv

CUSTOMERS = [
    ("C1", "ana@example.com", "10115", "Ana"),
    ("C2", "ben@example.com", "80331", "Ben"),
    ("C3", "chen@example.com", "20095", "Chen"),
]
# id, customer, status, total, delivered_on, address, refund_amount
ORDERS = [
    ("O-1001", "C1", "delivered", 59.0, "2026-09-21", "1 Elm St", 0.0),
    ("O-1002", "C1", "delivered", 120.0, "2026-08-17", "1 Elm St", 0.0),
    ("O-1003", "C1", "refunded", 25.0, "2026-09-20", "1 Elm St", 25.0),
    ("O-2001", "C2", "delivered", 35.0, "2026-09-25", "9 Oak Rd", 0.0),
    ("O-2002", "C2", "delivered", 80.0, "2026-09-12", "9 Oak Rd", 0.0),
    ("O-3001", "C3", "open", 42.0, None, "5 Pine Ave", 0.0),
    ("O-3002", "C3", "shipped", 18.0, None, "5 Pine Ave", 0.0),
]


@dataclass
class Task:
    id: str
    opening: str
    facts: dict
    expect: dict = field(default_factory=dict)  # order_id -> {column: new value}
    must_mention: str = ""

    def make_env(self) -> ShopEnv:
        return ShopEnv(CUSTOMERS, ORDERS)


ANA = {"email": "ana@example.com", "zip": "10115"}
BEN = {"email": "ben@example.com", "zip": "80331"}
CHEN = {"email": "chen@example.com", "zip": "20095"}

TASKS = [
    Task(
        "refund-ok",
        "My order arrived damaged and I want a refund.",
        {**ANA, "order_id": "O-1001"},
        {"O-1001": {"status": "refunded", "refund_amount": 59.0}},
    ),
    Task(
        "refund-late",
        "I'd like a refund please, I changed my mind.",
        {**ANA, "order_id": "O-1002"},
    ),
    Task(
        "refund-older",
        "I want a refund for one of my orders.",
        {**BEN, "order_id": "O-2002"},
        {"O-2002": {"status": "refunded", "refund_amount": 80.0}},
    ),
    Task(
        "address-open",
        "I need to change the delivery address on my order.",
        {**CHEN, "order_id": "O-3001", "address": "77 Birch Way"},
        {"O-3001": {"address": "77 Birch Way"}},
    ),
    Task(
        "address-shipped",
        "Please change the address on my order.",
        {**CHEN, "order_id": "O-3002", "address": "77 Birch Way"},
    ),
    Task(
        "wrong-zip", "Refund my last order please.", {**BEN, "zip": "99999", "order_id": "O-2001"}
    ),
    Task("already-refunded", "I want a refund for my order.", {**ANA, "order_id": "O-1003"}),
    Task(
        "other-customer",
        "Change the address on my order.",
        {**BEN, "order_id": "O-3001", "address": "1 New St"},
    ),
    Task(
        "status",
        "Where is my order? What's its status?",
        {**CHEN, "order_id": "O-3002"},
        must_mention="shipped",

steps.text: Write the checks: a diff of the orders table against the starting snapshot, compared with the expected changes; trajectory rules for writes before verification and writes the task did not need; and the answer check for the status task. Every reason maps to an error-analysis label.
Note why the trajectory rule matters: re-refunding an already refunded order leaves the table unchanged, so the end-state diff alone would miss it. The 'unneeded write' rule catches it.

Let new tasks test your reference agent too. When this project was written, the other-customer task (Ben asks to change an order that belongs to Chen) was added last, and the reference agent failed it: it verified Ben, then changed Chen's order, because it never checked ownership. The checks flagged a write on an unverified customer's order. The fix is policy rule 4 and the ownership check in RuleAgent; a benchmark that finds bugs in its own reference agent is doing its job.

phases.title: Agents
phases.goal: A reference agent, a sloppy agent with realistic mistakes, and an adapter for real models.

steps.text: Write the agents. RuleAgent follows the policy step by step; with faults it skips verification, guesses the newest order instead of asking, or ignores the refund rules, each with a given probability from a seeded generator. LLMAgent drives any model through a complete() function, and openai_compatible provides one for OpenAI-style endpoints.

Read the LLM system prompt: it is the policy plus two sentences. That is intentionally plain, so the benchmark measures the model and the tools, and so you can measure the effect of improving the prompt later.

Compare the two agent types: the rule agent can only do what it was written to do, which makes it a perfect reference for testing the benchmark itself, while the LLM agent shows what a real model does with the same tools and policy.

phases.title: Run, report and analyse
phases.goal: Results files per agent, a pass^k table, and failures labelled and read.

steps.text: Write the runner: every task, n trials, a fresh environment and user per trial, and one JSON line per trial with the reasons and labels.
Write the report: unbiased pass^k per task, the average over tasks, and failure category counts.

code.code:
# src/bench/report.py
"""pass^k per task and overall, plus failure categories.
uv run python -m bench.report results.jsonl"""

import json
import sys
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from math import comb


def pass_hat_k(n: int, c: int, k: int) -> float:
    """Unbiased estimate of P(all k of k fresh trials succeed) from n trials with c successes."""
    return comb(c, k) / comb(n, k)


def main() -> None:
    with open(sys.argv[1]) as f:
        rows = [json.loads(line) for line in f]
    by_task, cats = defaultdict(list), Counter()
    for r in rows:
        by_task[r["task"]].append(r["passed"])
        cats.update(r["categories"])
    ks = [k for k in (1, 2, 4, 8) if k <= min(len(v) for v in by_task.values())]
    print(f"{'task':18}" + "".join(f"{'pass^' + str(k):>9}" for k in ks))
    totals = defaultdict(list)
    for task, outcomes in by_task.items():
        n, c = len(outcomes), sum(outcomes)
        vals = [pass_hat_k(n, c, k) for k in ks]
        for k, v in zip(ks, vals):
            totals[k].append(v)
        print(f"{task:18}" + "".join(f"{v:9.2f}" for v in vals))
    print(f"{'ALL TASKS':18}" + "".join(f"{sum(totals[k]) / len(totals[k]):9.2f}" for k in ks))
    print("\nfailure categories:", dict(cats.most_common()) or "none")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

steps.text: Run the reference agent. Every task scores 1.00 at every k, which tests the benchmark itself: if the reference agent fails a task, the task, the check or the agent is wrong.

code.code:
uv run python -m bench.run --agent rule --trials 8 --out rule.jsonl
uv run python -m bench.report rule.jsonl

steps.text: Run the sloppy agent. Overall pass^1 is 0.82, but pass^4 is 0.49 and pass^8 is 0.33: an agent that usually works is rarely reliable across repeated attempts. The categories show unneeded writes and actions against policy dominate.

code.code:
uv run python -m bench.run --agent sloppy --trials 8 --out sloppy.jsonl
uv run python -m bench.report sloppy.jsonl

steps.text: Read the failures themselves, not just the counts.
Check efficiency alongside success: the median number of tool calls in passing trials. When you compare agents, a higher pass rate bought with many more calls may not be a win.

phases.title: Test the benchmark
phases.goal: Tests that prove the reference agent passes every task, each fault is caught with the right label, pass^k is correct, and the LLM loop and adapter work.

steps.text: Write the tests. The scripted complete() plays back tool calls, so the LLM agent loop is tested without a model; removing the verification step from the script must produce an 'unverified write'.

code.code:
# tests/test_bench.py
import json
import threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

import pytest

from bench.agents import LLMAgent, RuleAgent, openai_compatible
from bench.checks import category, check
from bench.report import pass_hat_k
from bench.tasks import TASKS
from bench.user import SimUser

BY_ID = {t.id: t for t in TASKS}


def trial(task_id, agent):
    task = BY_ID[task_id]
    env, user = task.make_env(), SimUser(task.opening, task.facts)
    final = agent.run(env, user)
    passed, reasons = check(task, env, final)
    return passed, sorted({category(r) for r in reasons}), env


@pytest.mark.parametrize("task_id", list(BY_ID))
def test_reference_agent_solves_every_task(task_id):
    assert trial(task_id, RuleAgent())[:2] == (True, [])


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "fault, task_id, expected",
    [
        ("skip_verification", "refund-ok", ["unverified write"]),
        (
            "guess_order",
            "refund-older",
            ["acted against policy", "missed change", "unneeded write"],
        ),
        ("ignore_policy", "refund-late", ["acted against policy", "unneeded write"]),
        ("ignore_policy", "already-refunded", ["unneeded write"]),
    ],
)
def test_each_fault_is_caught_and_labelled(fault, task_id, expected):
    passed, cats, _ = trial(task_id, RuleAgent({fault: 1.0}))
    assert not passed and cats == expected


def test_pass_hat_k():
    assert pass_hat_k(8, 8, 4) == 1.0
    assert pass_hat_k(8, 4, 2) == pytest.approx(6 / 28)
    assert pass_hat_k(8, 3, 4) == 0.0


def scripted(calls):
    """A fake complete() that plays back tool calls, one per model turn."""
    turns = iter(calls)

    def complete(messages, tools):
        name, args = next(turns)
        call = {"id": f"c{len(messages)}", "name": name, "args": args}
        return {"content": None, "tool_calls": [call]}

    return complete


GOOD_REFUND = [
    ("ask_user", {"question": "What is your email?"}),
    ("find_customer", {"email": "ana@example.com"}),
    ("ask_user", {"question": "And your zip code?"}),
    ("verify_identity", {"customer_id": "C1", "zip_code": "10115"}),
    ("ask_user", {"question": "Which order?"}),
    ("get_order", {"order_id": "O-1001"}),
    ("refund_order", {"order_id": "O-1001"}),
    ("respond", {"message": "Refunded in full."}),
]


def test_llm_agent_loop_with_scripted_model():
    assert trial("refund-ok", LLMAgent(scripted(GOOD_REFUND)))[:2] == (True, [])
    skipped = [c for c in GOOD_REFUND if c[0] != "verify_identity"]
    assert trial("refund-ok", LLMAgent(scripted(skipped)))[1] == ["unverified write"]


def test_openai_compatible_request_and_parsing():
    seen = {}

    class Stub(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
        def do_POST(self):
            seen["body"] = json.loads(self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"])))
            call = {
                "id": "x",
                "function": {"name": "get_order", "arguments": '{"order_id": "O-1"}'},
            }
            data = json.dumps({"choices": [{"message": {"content": None, "tool_calls": [call]}}]})
            self.send_response(200)
            self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
            self.end_headers()
            self.wfile.write(data.encode())

        def log_message(self, *a):
            pass

    server = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Stub)
    threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
    complete = openai_compatible(f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}/v1", "k", "m")
    out = complete([{"role": "assistant", "content": "", "tool_calls": None}], [{"name": "x"}])
    server.shutdown()
    assert "tool_calls" not in seen["body"]["messages"][0]
    assert out["tool_calls"] == [{"id": "x", "name": "get_order", "args": {"order_id": "O-1"}}]

steps.text: Run them. Sixteen tests pass in under a second.

phases.title: Benchmark a real model
phases.goal: pass^k and labelled failures for a real model, and one measured improvement.

steps.text: Point the LLM agent at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint with tool calling and run four trials per task (start small: each trial is a full conversation).

code.code:
export BENCH_BASE_URL="https://your-endpoint.example/v1"
export BENCH_MODEL="$YOUR_MODEL"
export BENCH_API_KEY="$YOUR_KEY"
uv run python -m bench.run --agent llm --trials 4 --out llm.jsonl
uv run python -m bench.report llm.jsonl

steps.text: Read every failed trial and its final message. Common real-model failures here are refunding outside the window when the customer insists, acting before verifying, and asking for everything at once in a way the simulated user does not understand.

Make one change aimed at the largest failure category (for example a clearer refund_order description saying to check the delivery date first, or a numbered procedure in the system prompt), re-run with the same trials, and compare pass^1 and pass^4. Keep the change only if it helps without new failure types.
Add two tasks that target the weakness you found, check that the reference agent passes them, and commit the benchmark so future prompt and model changes are measured on it.

troubleshooting.symptom: The reference agent fails a task you added
troubleshooting.fix: The task's expected end state or facts are wrong, or the simulated user cannot answer the agent's question. Fix the task first: the reference agent is the benchmark's own test.

troubleshooting.symptom: Results change between identical runs of the sloppy agent
troubleshooting.fix: Seeds must not depend on hash() of strings, which is randomised per process, and anything iterated from a set must be sorted. Both are handled in the code above.

troubleshooting.symptom: The LLM agent's turns go nowhere with replies like 'Sorry, I'm not sure what you need'
troubleshooting.fix: The simulated user answers one fact per question, matched by keywords (email, zip, order, address). Ask for one thing at a time, or extend SimUser with more patterns.

troubleshooting.symptom: HTTP 400 from the endpoint mentioning tool_calls
troubleshooting.fix: Some servers reject assistant messages with tool_calls set to null; the adapter strips None values, so check you are using openai_compatible and that the model supports tool calling.
